Les Amazighs : la commémoration du Print: The Amazigh people: commemorating the Amazigh Spring
Chaque année, le 20 avril célèbre la com: Every year on April 20, the Amazigh Spring is commemorated, a landmark period in Algeria's history. Thousands of people took to the streets demanding that their language, Tamazight, be made official and their culture recognized as part of Algerian identity. Independent since 1962, Algeria had faced no major opposition movement: the events of the Amazigh Spring in April 1980 were the first significant opposition to the establishment. The Amazigh are an ethnic group that has lived in North Africa for thousands of years. The assertion and affirmation of Amazigh culture are alive today in Algeria, and among Indigenous peoples throughout the region. In the face of the injustice and stigma the Amazigh community experiences across the region, the Amazigh Spring stands for the struggle against repressive policies in the countries where Amazigh communities live. FACTS: There are more than 30 million Amazigh people in North Africa The Tamazight language has its own ancient alphabet, Tifinagh The word “Berber” is pejorative, as it comes from a colonial name, “Barbaros,” meaning “foreigner” or “barbarian.” Today, the preferred terms are “Amazigh” (m), “Tamazight” or “Imazighen” (plural), meaning “free people” An ancient tradition in Amazigh culture is tattooing, practised for many reasons, such as an upcoming marriage or belonging to a tribe SOURCES: https://www.ipacc.org.za/north-africa/

Islamophobie et antisémitisme : deux pos: Islamophobia and antisemitism: two positions abolished in Ottawa
Ottawa a aboli deux postes fédéraux dédi: Ottawa has abolished two federal positions dedicated to fighting Islamophobia and antisemitism, replacing them with an advisory council. Yet in 2023, Canada had created a federal position explicitly devoted to fighting Islamophobia — a first at that institutional level. Coming six days after the ninth anniversary of the Quebec City mosque attack, the announcement surprised many. While some elected officials in Quebec welcomed the decision, it has raised serious concerns within the communities affected. On social media, Muslim researchers, journalists and activists expressed their disappointment, recalling that the position was created in the wake of deadly attacks on Muslims in Canada and that it represented institutional recognition of Islamophobia as a real, documented phenomenon. Jewish organizations, for their part, also voiced concerns, fearing that the loss of a position dedicated to fighting antisemitism would dilute efforts at a time when antisemitic acts are on the rise. It remains to be seen whether the new committee will meet communities' expectations. Aya Boucenna explains.

Zeinab Diab, chercheuse indépendante, dé: Zeinab Diab, an independent researcher, unpacks the political and human stakes of Bill 21 and Quebec's secularism laws. Drawing on her research and on the testimony of women directly affected, she analyzes the court rulings, including the case before the Supreme Court, and how the debate has shifted from the real consequences to the “notwithstanding clause” alone. She also discusses the positions of the political parties, including Québec solidaire, and what she describes as a “soft left” in the face of Islamophobia. Finally, she challenges Muslim communities on their relationship with elected officials and calls for more organized forms of resistance, to make the impact of these laws visible and to push back against a nationalist project that, in her view, relies on restricting rights and making Muslim women invisible.
